Homework 04 — Lasso and Variable Selection

Simulation, coordinate descent, and diabetes prediction

All numerical results below were computed in Python. The original assignment, course-provided solution, and data are preserved alongside this report. Frequencies are proportions, so 0.520 means selection in 52% of the 200 repetitions. The full analysis code is included in the appendix. This report was prepared with AI assistance.

Question 1: Signal strength and correlated substitutes

Simulation and fitting conventions

I used NumPy’s default_rng(43246). In each repetition I drew X1X_1, ZZ, the eight remaining covariate vectors, and the noise vector, in that order, exactly following the question’s generating equation. For every generated dataset I fitted all four penalties before generating the next dataset. Each column was transformed using

zij=xij−x‾jsj,sj2=1n∑i(xij−x‾j)2.z_{ij}=\frac{x_{ij}-\bar x_j}{s_j},\qquad s_j^2=\frac1n\sum_i(x_{ij}-\bar x_j)^2.

The centered response was fitted with Lasso(alpha=lam, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-10, max_iter=100000). In scikit-learn, alpha specifies λ\lambda; Lasso does not automatically standardize columns. I therefore standardized them explicitly before fitting. Setting fit_intercept=False here is appropriate because the intercept has already been fitted separately as y‾\bar y; it is not penalized. The objective on the standardized design is

12n∥ỹ−Zb∥22+λ∥b∥1.\frac{1}{2n}\|\widetilde y-Zb\|_2^2+\lambda\|b\|_1.

I stored original-scale slopes β̂j=bj/sj\widehat\beta_j=b_j/s_j in an array of shape (200,10,4)(200,10,4). The corresponding original-scale intercept is β̂0=y‾−∑jx‾jβ̂j\widehat\beta_0=\bar y-\sum_j\bar x_j\widehat\beta_j. Selection means |β̂j|>10−8|\widehat\beta_j|>10^{-8}.

All 800 lasso fits converged without a convergence warning. The largest iteration count was 11,153, below the limit of 100,000; the maximum reported dual gap was 1.19×10−111.19\times10^{-11}. Convergence warnings are treated as errors in the script rather than suppressed.

Covariate 0.08 0.12 0.18 0.24
X1 0.115 0.097 0.068 0.040
X2 0.101 0.080 0.054 0.034
X3 0.211 0.172 0.118 0.072
X4 0.071 0.043 0.016 0.004

Increasing the penalty generally lowers both selection frequency and mean absolute slope. The independent stronger signal X3X_3 remains selected more often than X4X_4. Noise variables become rare as the penalty grows. The frequency for X1X_1 is unchanged between the first two penalties, illustrating that individual-variable selection need not decrease strictly along a lasso path, especially when predictors can substitute for one another. The general shrinkage trend concerns these observed summaries, not a guarantee of monotonicity for every individual coefficient.

(b) Correlated-pair outcomes

Penalty Only X1 Only X2 Both Neither
0.080 0.485 0.460 0.035 0.020
0.120 0.495 0.435 0.025 0.045
0.180 0.490 0.380 0.005 0.125
0.240 0.405 0.335 0.005 0.255

The marginal frequencies are similar in broad scale: for X1X_1 they are 0.520, 0.520, 0.495, and 0.410, while for X2X_2 they are 0.495, 0.460, 0.385, and 0.340. The predictors have symmetric population roles: the same variance, the same true coefficient, and almost identical information. The finite sample experiment need not give identical frequencies; for example, the gap is 0.110 at λ=0.18\lambda=0.18. Repetition-level sampling fluctuations and tiny differences in the observed scores decide which variable is retained.

Selecting exactly one member is overwhelmingly more common than selecting both. As λ\lambda rises, selecting neither increases from 2.0% to 25.5%, while selecting both falls from 3.5% to 0.5%. Individual outcome probabilities are not all strictly monotone: the only-X1X_1 outcome first rises slightly and then declines.

To see why a generating coefficient can be omitted, imagine identical columns and two nonnegative coefficients with fixed sum cc. Their predictions depend only on cc, and their lasso penalty is λ(|b1|+|b2|)=λc\lambda(|b_1|+|b_2|)=\lambda c regardless of how the sum is allocated. There is no penalty advantage to sharing the coefficient. With nearly identical columns, a small difference in fit can favor allocating the signal to just one member. Sparsity therefore need not recover every generating variable when signals are highly redundant.

(c) Strong signals, weak signals, and noise

Penalty X3X_3 X4X_4 Mean among X5,…,X10X_5,\ldots,X_{10}
0.08 0.980 0.755 0.390
0.12 0.970 0.610 0.202
0.18 0.865 0.325 0.058
0.24 0.670 0.115 0.013

The 0.30 signal in X3X_3 survives the threshold more often than the 0.15 signal in X4X_4. Increasing λ\lambda screens out noise but also removes weak genuine signals; at 0.24, X4X_4 is retained in only 11.5% of runs. Random empirical associations can retain noise variables, especially at low penalties.

A fitted zero does not prove a zero population coefficient: X1X_1 and X2X_2 each have a nonzero generating coefficient yet either is frequently omitted. A selected coefficient does not prove unique importance either: the other member of this pair can provide almost the same predictive information. Selection is conditional on the data, penalty, and other available predictors.

Question 2: Elastic net with an equal penalty mix

I reused the exact same 200 generated datasets as Question 1. This is equivalent to resetting the seed and repeating the same draw sequence, and ensures that differences reflect the fitting method rather than a new simulation. ElasticNet(alpha=lam, l1_ratio=0.5, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-10, max_iter=100000) uses the objective

12n∥ỹ−Zb∥22+λ(0.5∥b∥1+0.52∥b∥22).\frac{1}{2n}\|\widetilde y-Zb\|_2^2+ \lambda\left(0.5\|b\|_1+\frac{0.5}{2}\|b\|_2^2\right).

Thus Python’s l1_ratio is the question’s mixing parameter, while Python’s alpha is the overall penalty. Scaling and conversion back to original slopes match Question 1. All 800 elastic-net fits converged; the maximum iteration count was 259 and the largest dual gap was 1.40×10−111.40\times10^{-11}.

(a) Selection frequencies

Covariate 0.08 0.12 0.18 0.24
X1 0.975 0.970 0.955 0.925
X2 0.960 0.975 0.970 0.945
X3 0.995 0.995 0.975 0.970
X4 0.880 0.820 0.725 0.600
X5 0.640 0.485 0.350 0.210
X6 0.660 0.525 0.370 0.200
X7 0.665 0.510 0.325 0.185
X8 0.660 0.530 0.355 0.220
X9 0.645 0.515 0.320 0.200
X10 0.650 0.530 0.315 0.205

Selection frequencies increase for every covariate at all four penalties relative to lasso. The most pronounced changes are for the correlated pair, particularly at the largest penalty: X1X_1 rises from 0.410 to 0.925 and X2X_2 from 0.340 to 0.945. The weaker independent signal also benefits: X4X_4 rises from 0.115 to 0.600 at that penalty. Noise selection increases as well, so greater retention is not by itself evidence of better variable recovery.

(b) Correlated-pair outcomes and grouping

Penalty Only X1 Only X2 Both Neither
0.080 0.035 0.020 0.940 0.005
0.120 0.010 0.015 0.960 0.015
0.180 0.010 0.025 0.945 0.020
0.240 0.005 0.025 0.920 0.050

Both members are now retained together in 92.0%–96.0% of repetitions, compared with only 0.5%–3.5% under lasso. This is strong joint retention, but it is not perfect selection in every dataset. At the largest penalty, 5% of runs omit both.

For identical columns and fixed coefficient sum cc, the squared penalty is minimized by equal allocation:

b12+b22=c22+(b1−b2)22≥c22.b_1^2+b_2^2 =\frac{c^2}{2}+\frac{(b_1-b_2)^2}{2}\geq\frac{c^2}{2}.

The additional squared penalty therefore favors sharing signal between highly correlated columns. In standardized coordinate descent, elastic net updates a coefficient as S(aj,λ/2)/(1+λ/2)S(a_j,\lambda/2)/(1+\lambda/2); this shows both the weaker threshold and the additional smooth shrinkage.

(c) Noise screening

Penalty Lasso: mean noise selection Elastic net: mean noise selection Elastic net: both pair members
0.08 0.390 0.653 0.940
0.12 0.202 0.516 0.960
0.18 0.058 0.339 0.945
0.24 0.013 0.203 0.920

Noise selection still decreases as the penalty increases. At the same numerical λ\lambda, however, elastic net has an ℓ1\ell_1 threshold of λ/2\lambda/2 rather than λ\lambda, so it screens less aggressively than lasso. At 0.18 and 0.24, it usually retains both correlated predictors while excluding most noise variables: the mean excluded proportions are 66.1% and 79.7%, respectively. Here “most” means the average proportion of noise variables excluded, not that every repetition excludes every noise variable. At 0.12, fewer than half are excluded on average.

Question 3: Coordinate descent and the lasso path

(a) Implementation and convergence

I used default_rng(43247), drew each of the three covariate vectors and then the noise vector, and standardized with divisor 100. The response was centered. Starting with zero slopes, I traversed the requested descending penalty grid and used the preceding solution as the next starting vector.

For coordinate jj, the partial residual and update were

r−j=ỹ−Zb+zjbj,aj=zj𝖳r−j100,bj←sign⁡(aj)(|aj|−λ)+.r_{-j}=\widetilde y-Zb+z_jb_j,\qquad a_j=\frac{z_j^{\mathsf T}r_{-j}}{100},\qquad b_j\leftarrow \operatorname{sign}(a_j)(|a_j|-\lambda)_+.

I updated coefficients immediately in cyclic order and stopped only after a full cycle had maximum coefficient change below 10−1010^{-10}. The appendix contains the complete hand-written loop; package fitting was used only as an independent check.

lambda X1 X2 X3 cycles
2.500000 0.000000 -0.000000 0.000000 1
2.000000 0.000000 -0.000000 0.000000 1
1.500000 0.000000 -0.125150 0.000000 2
1.000000 0.000000 -0.625150 0.000000 2
0.600000 0.185593 -1.030712 0.000000 5
0.400000 0.391772 -1.236892 0.000000 5
0.250000 0.546407 -1.391526 0.000000 5
0.150000 0.649497 -1.494616 0.000000 5
0.080000 0.721660 -1.566779 0.000000 5
0.030000 0.773204 -1.618324 -0.000000 5

All ten fits converged within five cycles. Coefficients are on the standardized covariate scale, and the separately fitted intercept is 1.285858. The largest KKT residual was 7.99×10−157.99\times10^{-15}, and every slope vector agreed with an independent scikit-learn lasso fit within absolute tolerance 10−810^{-8}.

The initial score vector is approximately (0.754702,−1.625150,0.262903)(0.754702,-1.625150,0.262903), giving

λmax=∥Z𝖳ỹ100∥∞=1.625150.\lambda_{\max}=\left\|\frac{Z^{\mathsf T}\widetilde y}{100}\right\|_\infty =1.625150.

The slopes are all zero at 2.5 and 2.0, the two grid values at or above this threshold. The zero solution satisfies the KKT inequalities precisely when every absolute score is at most λ\lambda.

(b) Path and entry order

As the penalty decreases, X2X_2 enters first (at 1.5 on the supplied grid), followed by X1X_1 (at 0.6). The third covariate never enters on this grid. This is consistent with the true absolute coefficients 2, 1, and 0, respectively. Entry is actually governed by empirical partial scores, so true coefficient magnitude alone does not guarantee this order in every random dataset.

(c) Smallest penalty versus least squares

Fit on standardized predictors b1b_1 b2b_2 b3b_3
Lasso, λ=0.03\lambda=0.03 0.773204 -1.618324 0.000000
Least squares 0.806363 -1.650248 -0.012041

In this run, X3X_3 is still zero at the smallest requested penalty. Its nonzero least-squares estimate reflects finite-sample noise, not a population signal. The small positive penalty keeps the two strong slopes close to their OLS values while shrinking them toward zero and thresholding the weak third slope exactly to zero. They are not identical because λ=0.03\lambda=0.03 still imposes a penalty. For this full-rank design the lasso solution approaches OLS as λ\lambda approaches zero; sufficiently smaller penalties would eventually allow the nonzero OLS coefficient for X3X_3 to emerge.

Question 4: Diabetes prediction

Training, validation, and penalty conventions

I matched the supplied row_id values to the data rows and used the provided 353 training observations, 89 test observations, and ten training fold labels. For each method, GridSearchCV evaluated the same 61 penalties np.logspace(-4, 2, 61) using PredefinedSplit and negative MSE scoring. I report positive MSE, averaged equally over the ten validation folds.

Each fit used a Pipeline with StandardScaler followed by the regression model. The scaler learned means and divisor-nn scales only from the current fitting observations. With fit_intercept=True, each estimator centers the response internally on those same fitting observations and fits an unpenalized intercept. Validation and test predictions use the fitted training transformations.

Lasso, Ridge, and ElasticNet(l1_ratio=0.5) select the three penalty families. The tabulated penalty is the scikit-learn alpha parameter. Lasso and elastic net use the normalized objectives given above, whereas Ridge minimizes ∥y−b0−Zb∥22+𝚊𝚕𝚙𝚑𝚊∥b∥22\|y-b_0-Zb\|_2^2+\texttt{alpha}\|b\|_2^2. Consequently these numerical penalties are package parameters, not directly comparable measures of shrinkage across methods. I used the assignment’s specified Python grids without rescaling ridge’s parameter.

Cross-validation results

Method Penalty CV MSE Fold SE
Lasso 0.100000 3071.246869 240.352677
Ridge 0.501187 3073.485775 242.146754
Elastic net 0.003162 3073.448712 242.100086

The shading in each plot is plus or minus one standard error, calculated as the sample standard deviation of the ten fold MSEs divided by 10\sqrt{10}. This is a descriptive fold-variability summary, not an independence-based confidence interval. Selection uses the minimum mean CV MSE, not the one-standard-error rule.

Lasso at penalty 0.1 has the smallest minimum CV MSE, 3071.247, and is therefore the selected method. The other minima are only about 2.2 MSE units higher. This small numerical advantage determines the requested choice; it does not provide strong evidence that lasso would consistently outperform the alternatives.

Final test assessment

After choosing lasso using training CV, I refitted its scaler and coefficients on all 353 training observations. I then evaluated this selected fit once on the 89 test observations:

MSE⁡test=189∑i∈test(yi−ŷi)2=2732.4104.\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}} =\frac1{89}\sum_{i\in\mathrm{test}}(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2 =\boxed{2732.4104}.

No test errors from the other methods were used to choose or revise the model. The test MSE being lower than CV MSE is compatible with variation in the held-out samples and fitting on a larger training sample in the final fit.

Sources and reproducibility

  • Week 4 course page and its homework ZIP: assignment and supplied diabetes data/folds.
  • scikit-learn ElasticNet documentation: penalty and mixing-parameter conventions.
  • scikit-learn Ridge documentation: ridge objective and intercept convention.

The course-provided solutions-04.qmd is retained as downloaded; the computations in this report come from analysis-04.py. Numerical runs use NumPy 2.2.2 and scikit-learn 1.9.1. Random-number generators differ across languages, so simulation numbers need not match the supplied R solution.

To reproduce from this directory, run:

python analysis-04.py
python build-report-04.py
quarto render homework-04.qmd

The results/ directory contains slope arrays, summary CSVs, convergence checks, figures, CV fold errors, and final test predictions. The rendered HTML embeds its resources and is the submission artifact.

Complete analysis code

"""Reproduce Homework 04: python analysis-04.py (run from any directory)."""
from pathlib import Path
import json
import warnings
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import sklearn
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso, ElasticNet, Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, PredefinedSplit
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.exceptions import ConvergenceWarning

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
OUT = ROOT / 'results'
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
warnings.filterwarnings('error', category=ConvergenceWarning)
plt.rcParams.update({'figure.dpi': 150, 'font.size': 10})
penalties = np.array([.08, .12, .18, .24])
names = [f'X{j}' for j in range(1, 11)]
summary = {'numpy': np.__version__, 'sklearn': sklearn.__version__}

def savefig(name):
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(OUT / f'{name}.png', bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.close()

# Reusing each generated dataset gives exact pairing of the two procedures.
rng = np.random.default_rng(43246)
coefs = {m: np.zeros((200, 10, 4)) for m in ['lasso', 'elastic_net']}
iterations = {m: [] for m in coefs}
gaps = {m: [] for m in coefs}
for rep in range(200):
    x1 = rng.standard_normal(120)
    z = rng.standard_normal(120)
    rest = rng.standard_normal((8, 120)).T
    x = np.column_stack([x1, .999*x1 + np.sqrt(1-.999**2)*z, rest])
    y = x @ np.array([.15,.15,.30,.15,0,0,0,0,0,0]) + rng.standard_normal(120)
    scale = x.std(axis=0, ddof=0)
    xs = (x-x.mean(axis=0))/scale
    yc = y-y.mean()
    for k, lam in enumerate(penalties):
        for method in coefs:
            cls = Lasso if method == 'lasso' else ElasticNet
            extra = {} if method == 'lasso' else {'l1_ratio': .5}
            model = cls(alpha=lam, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-10,
                        max_iter=100000, selection='cyclic', **extra).fit(xs, yc)
            assert model.n_iter_ < 100000
            coefs[method][rep, :, k] = model.coef_/scale
            iterations[method].append(int(model.n_iter_))
            gaps[method].append(float(model.dual_gap_))

for method, b in coefs.items():
    np.save(OUT / f'{method}-slopes.npy', b)
    selected = np.abs(b) > 1e-8
    freq = selected.mean(axis=0)
    magnitude = np.abs(b).mean(axis=0)
    for label, values in [('frequency',freq), ('magnitude',magnitude)]:
        pd.DataFrame(values, index=names, columns=penalties).to_csv(OUT / f'{method}-{label}.csv')
        if method == 'elastic_net' and label == 'magnitude':
            continue
        plt.figure(figsize=(8,4.6))
        for k, lam in enumerate(penalties):
            plt.plot(names, values[:,k], 'o-', label=f'λ = {lam:.2f}')
        plt.xlabel('Covariate')
        plt.ylabel('Selection frequency' if label == 'frequency' else 'Mean absolute slope (original scale)')
        if label == 'frequency': plt.ylim(-.025,1.025)
        plt.title(('Lasso' if method == 'lasso' else 'Elastic net (mix = 0.5)') + ': 200 repetitions')
        plt.legend(ncol=2)
        savefig(f'{method}-{label}')
    first, second = selected[:,0,:], selected[:,1,:]
    pair = np.array([(first & ~second).mean(0), (~first & second).mean(0),
                     (first & second).mean(0), (~first & ~second).mean(0)]).T
    assert np.allclose(pair.sum(axis=1), 1)
    pd.DataFrame(pair, index=penalties, columns=['Only X1','Only X2','Both','Neither']).to_csv(OUT/f'{method}-pair.csv')
    summary[method] = {'fits':len(iterations[method]),'max_iterations':max(iterations[method]),
                       'max_dual_gap':max(gaps[method]), 'noise_frequency':freq[4:].mean(0).tolist()}

# A hand-written warm-start coordinate descent on standardized slopes.
rng = np.random.default_rng(43247)
x = rng.standard_normal((3,100)).T
y = 1.5 + x[:,0] - 2*x[:,1] + rng.standard_normal(100)
xs = (x-x.mean(0))/x.std(0,ddof=0)
yc = y-y.mean()
grid = np.array([2.5,2,1.5,1,.6,.4,.25,.15,.08,.03])
b = np.zeros(3)
rows = []
for lam in grid:
    for cycle in range(1,100001):
        old = b.copy()
        for j in range(3):
            residual_without_j = yc-xs@b+xs[:,j]*b[j]
            score = xs[:,j]@residual_without_j/100
            b[j] = np.sign(score)*max(abs(score)-lam,0)
        change = np.max(np.abs(b-old))
        if change < 1e-10:
            break
    else:
        raise RuntimeError('Coordinate descent failed to converge')
    score = xs.T@(yc-xs@b)/100
    active = np.abs(b)>1e-8
    violations = np.where(active, np.abs(score-lam*np.sign(b)), np.maximum(np.abs(score)-lam,0))
    reference = Lasso(alpha=lam,fit_intercept=False,tol=1e-12,max_iter=100000).fit(xs,yc)
    assert np.max(violations)<1e-8
    assert np.allclose(b,reference.coef_,atol=1e-8,rtol=0)
    rows.append([lam,*b,cycle,change,float(max(violations))])
path = pd.DataFrame(rows,columns=['lambda','X1','X2','X3','cycles','last_change','KKT_error'])
path.to_csv(OUT/'coordinate-path.csv',index=False)
lmax = float(np.max(np.abs(xs.T@yc/100)))
assert np.all(path.loc[path['lambda']>=lmax,names[:3]].to_numpy()==0)
ols = np.linalg.lstsq(xs,yc,rcond=None)[0]
summary['q3'] = {'lambda_max':lmax, 'intercept_standardized':float(y.mean()), 'ols':ols.tolist(),
                 'initial_scores':(xs.T@yc/100).tolist(),'max_KKT_error':float(path.KKT_error.max())}
plt.figure(figsize=(8,4.6))
for name in names[:3]: plt.plot(np.log(grid),path[name],'o-',label=name)
plt.axhline(0,color='gray',lw=.7)
plt.xlabel('log(λ) (natural logarithm; penalty decreases toward the left)')
plt.ylabel('Slope on standardized covariates')
plt.legend()
savefig('coordinate-path')

# Fixed folds, with preprocessing learned afresh in each training fold.
data = pd.read_csv(ROOT/'data/diabetes.csv')
split = pd.read_csv(ROOT/'data/diabetes-split-folds.csv')
assert np.array_equal(split.row_id,np.arange(1,len(data)+1))
train = split['split'].eq('train').to_numpy()
assert train.sum()==353 and (~train).sum()==89
folds = split.loc[train,'cv_fold'].astype(int).to_numpy()-1
assert set(folds)==set(range(10))
Xtrain = data.drop(columns='y').loc[train]
ytrain = data.loc[train,'y']
grid = np.logspace(-4,2,61)
models = {'Lasso':Lasso(tol=1e-10,max_iter=100000),
          'Ridge':Ridge(solver='svd'),
          'Elastic net':ElasticNet(l1_ratio=.5,tol=1e-10,max_iter=100000)}
tuned = {}
comparison = []
for method, model in models.items():
    # fit_intercept=True centers y using only the current fitting observations.
    pipe = Pipeline([('scale',StandardScaler()),('model',model)])
    search = GridSearchCV(pipe,{'model__alpha':grid},cv=PredefinedSplit(folds),
                          scoring='neg_mean_squared_error',refit=False,error_score='raise')
    search.fit(Xtrain,ytrain)
    means = -search.cv_results_['mean_test_score']
    fold_mse = -np.column_stack([search.cv_results_[f'split{i}_test_score'] for i in range(10)])
    se = fold_mse.std(axis=1,ddof=1)/np.sqrt(10)
    best = search.best_index_
    comparison.append([method,float(grid[best]),float(means[best]),float(se[best])])
    tuned[method] = pipe.set_params(**search.best_params_)
    slug = method.lower().replace(' ','-')
    pd.DataFrame({'alpha':grid,'mean_mse':means,'se':se}).to_csv(OUT/f'cv-{slug}.csv',index=False)
    np.save(OUT/f'cv-{slug}-fold-mse.npy',fold_mse)
    plt.figure(figsize=(8,4.6))
    plt.semilogx(grid,means,'-',color='#155e75')
    plt.fill_between(grid,means-se,means+se,alpha=.18,color='#155e75',label='± 1 fold SE')
    plt.axvline(grid[best],color='#b45309',ls='--',label=f'Selected α = {grid[best]:.6g}')
    plt.xlabel('Penalty (scikit-learn alpha)')
    plt.ylabel('Mean validation MSE')
    plt.title(method+' — supplied ten folds')
    plt.legend()
    savefig(f'cv-{slug}')
comparison = pd.DataFrame(comparison,columns=['Method','Penalty','CV MSE','Fold SE'])
comparison.to_csv(OUT/'cv-comparison.csv',index=False)
winner = comparison.loc[comparison['CV MSE'].idxmin(),'Method']
final = tuned[winner].fit(Xtrain,ytrain)
# Access test outcomes only after choosing the procedure using training CV.
pred = final.predict(data.drop(columns='y').loc[~train])
test_mse = float(np.mean((data.loc[~train,'y'].to_numpy()-pred)**2))
